---
title: "Plea bargaining (asymmetric information)"
toc: true
---

## What it is
Plea bargaining is modeled as bargaining under uncertainty:
- prosecutor offers a plea sentence,
- defendant accepts or goes to trial,
- trial outcomes are uncertain and costly.

A core academic theme: **selection into trial** and **asymmetric information**.

---

## Canonical setup (two types)
Defendant type $\theta\in\{L,H\}$ with prior $\Pr(H)=\pi$.
Type affects probability of conviction at trial:
- $\Pr(\text{conviction}|\theta=L)=p_L$
- $\Pr(\text{conviction}|\theta=H)=p_H$
with $0<p_L<p_H<1$.

Trial sentence if convicted: $T>0$.  
Prosecutor offers plea sentence $x$ (certain if accepted).  
Trial cost to prosecutor: $c_P>0$. Trial cost to defendant: $c_D>0$.

Defendant expected cost of trial (type $\theta$):
$$
\text{TrialCost}(\theta)=p_\theta T + c_D.
$$
Accept plea iff:
$$
x \le p_\theta T + c_D.
$$

Prosecutor payoff:
- if plea accepted: $x$
- if trial: expected sentence $p_\theta T$ minus cost $c_P$.

---

## Solved equilibrium pattern: separating via one offer (screening)
Suppose prosecutor wants:
- type $H$ to accept the plea,
- type $L$ to reject and go to trial.

For this to happen, choose $x$ such that:
- $H$ accepts: $x \le p_H T + c_D$
- $L$ rejects: $x > p_L T + c_D$

So any $x$ in:
$$
(p_L T + c_D,\; p_H T + c_D]
$$
induces the intended separation.

Prosecutor then compares expected payoff under this policy:
- From type $H$: gets $x$
- From type $L$ (trial): gets $p_L T - c_P$

Expected payoff:
$$
\pi x + (1-\pi)(p_L T - c_P).
$$

A common selection result: when the gap $p_H-p_L$ is large enough, a single plea offer can screen types.

---

## Predictions (qualitative)
- Higher defendant trial cost $c_D$ increases acceptance of pleas (both types).
- Higher prosecutor trial cost $c_P$ increases reliance on plea offers (lower $x$ may still be attractive).
- Stronger evidence (higher $p_\theta$) increases willingness to accept pleas (especially high type).

---

## Interpretation and links
- Observed trial cases are selected: they are not “random disputes.”
- Plea policy can change recorded outcomes (conviction rates, sentence distributions) without changing underlying behavior.
